And as I came into the cloud of London I met a friend of mine who actually is in a bank, and submitted these suggestions in rhyme to him for use among his colleagues. But he was not very hopeful about the matter. It was not (he assured me) that he underrated the verses, or in any sense lamented their lack of polish. No; it was rather, he felt, an indefinable something in the very atmosphere of the society in which we live that makes it spiritually difficult to sing in banks. And I think he must be right; though the matter is very mysterious. I may observe here that I think there must be some mistake in the calculations of the Socialists. They put down all our distress, not to a moral tone, but to the chaos of private enterprise. Now, banks are private; but post-offices are Socialistic: therefore I naturally expected that the post-office would fall into the collectivist idea of a chorus. Judge of my surprise when the lady in my local post-office (whom I urged to sing) dismissed the idea with far more coldness than the bank clerk had done. She seemed indeed, to be in a considerably greater state of depression than he. Should any one suppose that this was the effect of the verses themselves, it is only fair to say that the specimen verse of the Post-Office Hymn ran thus:

“O’er London our letters are shaken like snow, Our wires o’er the world like the thunderbolts go. The news that may marry a maiden in Sark, Or kill an old lady in Finsbury Park.”

Chorus (with a swing of joy and energy):

“Or kill an old lady in Finsbury Park.”

And the more I thought about the matter the more painfully certain it seemed that the most important and typical modern things could not be done with a chorus. One could not, for instance, be a great financier and sing; because the essence of being a great financier is that you keep quiet. You could not even in many modern circles be a public man and sing; because in those circles the essence of being a public man is that you do nearly everything in private. Nobody would imagine a chorus of money-lenders. Every one knows the story of the solicitors’ corps of volunteers who, when the Colonel on the battlefield cried “Charge!” all said simultaneously, “Six-and-eightpence.” Men can sing while charging in a military, but hardly in a legal sense. And at the end of my reflections I had really got no further than the sub-conscious feeling of my friend the bank-clerk—that there is something spiritually suffocating about our life; not about our laws merely, but about our life. Bank-clerks are without songs, not because they are poor, but because they are sad. Sailors are much poorer. As I passed homewards I passed a little tin building of some religious sort, which was shaken with shouting as a trumpet is torn with its own tongue. THEY were singing anyhow; and I had for an instant a fancy I had often had before: that with us the super-human is the only place where you can find the human. Human nature is hunted and has fled into sanctuary.

message.content:
As I entered the haze of London, I encountered a friend who works at a bank, to whom I presented these poetic suggestions intended for his colleagues. However, he expressed a lack of optimism regarding the matter. It wasn't that he underestimated the quality of the verses or regretted their rough edges; rather, he sensed an elusive quality in the very fabric of our societal environment that makes it spiritually challenging for individuals to express themselves through song within banks. I believe he is onto something, although the reasoning remains enigmatic. I must note, too, that I believe the Socialists may have erred in their assessments. They attribute our societal woes not to a moral failing but to the disarray of private enterprise. While banks operate within this private realm, post-offices exemplify a more collectivist approach; thus, I expected the post-office to embrace a communal spirit. Imagine my astonishment when the woman at my local post-office, whom I encouraged to sing, responded with even greater indifference than the bank clerk had shown. In fact, she appeared to be in a deeper state of gloom than he.

If anyone were to think that the verses themselves were the cause of her disinterest, it is only fair to mention that the sample line from the Post-Office Hymn read as follows: 

“O’er London our letters are shaken like snow,  
Our wires o’er the world like the thunderbolts go.  
The news that may marry a maiden in Sark,  
Or kill an old lady in Finsbury Park.”  

The accompanying chorus, infused with exuberance, declared:  

“Or kill an old lady in Finsbury Park.”  

The more I contemplated this situation, the more it became clear that some of the most significant and quintessentially modern endeavors seem incompatible with the idea of a chorus. For instance, one cannot be a prominent financier while engaging in song, as the very nature of successful finance demands discretion and silence. Moreover, in many contemporary circles, being a public figure often entails conducting one’s affairs in private, leaving little room for the act of singing. The notion of a chorus composed of money-lenders would be utterly absurd. We are all familiar with the tale of the volunteers among solicitors who, when ordered to "Charge!" on the battlefield, all concurrently replied, “Six-and-eightpence.” It appears that while men can sing in the context of military charge, doing so in a legal framework is virtually impossible.

By the conclusion of my reflections, I found myself grappling with the same underlying sentiment as my bank-clerk friend: there exists something spiritually stifling about our existence—this goes beyond mere laws and penetrates the essence of our lives. Bank clerks lack songs not due to poverty, but rather from a deeper sadness. In stark contrast, sailors endure far greater hardships. On my way home, I passed a small tin structure of a religious nature, which resonated with boisterous singing, reminiscent of a trumpet's clarion call. In that moment, I was struck by a recurring thought: it seems that in our society, the extraordinary is often the only refuge where one can discover the essence of humanity. Human nature appears to be relentlessly pursued, retreating into a sanctuary away from the harsh realities of life.
